name: carbonx_ask_dna
description: Ask Carbon-X a question about DNA sequences you supply. It is a 14.8B language model trained jointly on DNA and English: give it named sequences and a question and it answers in prose, with its reasoning. MEASURED HERE on 50 balanced ClinVar missense SNVs: 80% at an 8,001-base window and 76% at 1,001, against 52% at 55, so GIVE IT THOUSANDS OF BASES AROUND THE SITE, not tens -- at 55 bases it calls almost everything pathogenic. The two long windows are not distinguishable at this sample size; the short one is clearly worse. The window is still an instability: the verdict changes on 8 of 50 variants between 1,001 and 8,001 bases with no accuracy gain to show for it, so treat a single call as one opinion rather than a classification. Variant effect is its measured strength. It reads DNA accurately but not exactly -- 98-99 residues per 100 correct when translating, and almost never a whole 100-residue protein right -- so do not use it to transcribe. Organism group measured 4 of 8 here against the 93.2% upstream reports, and splice sites and histone marks are weak upstream too; it miscounts bases and coordinates, and it was not trained to design sequences. The answer is a model prediction, NOT clinically validated, and must not drive a medical decision. Sequences are DNA only; 'sequences' is required, because this tool answers questions about DNA rather than acting as a general assistant. The prompt is limited to about 7,168 tokens (roughly 43 kbp of DNA); a longer one is refused by name with its real token count.

question.description: What to ask about the sequences. Put everything in one question: Carbon-X was trained and evaluated with the sequence and the question in a single message. For a variant, give the position and the reference and alternate base, computed in code rather than left to the model to locate.

sequences.description: The DNA to ask about, as name -> sequence. Names are how the question refers to them ('reference', 'variant', 'promoter'). IUPAC ambiguity codes are accepted but cost resolution: only A, C, G and T form 6-mer tokens, and any 6-mer containing another character collapses into one <oov> token. SIZE THEM FOR THE QUESTION: for a variant, pass the reference and alternate as windows of a thousand bases or more centred on the site. A 55-base window scored 52% here where 8,001 bases scored 80%, and short windows fail asymmetrically -- specificity collapsed to 7 of 25 while sensitivity held. At most 16 sequences.

context.description: What is already known: gene, strand, assembly, coordinates, annotations. Placed before the question. Upstream's strongest prompting advice -- without it the model may invent a sequence's identity or function.

max_tokens.description: Ceiling on the answer, 1 to 4096. Generation measured about 12-14 tokens per second on the verified card, so this is the main thing that sets how long a call takes. The reply says whether the answer was truncated.

seed.description: Random seed. Carbon-X's published results use sampling (temperature 0.6, top-p 0.95, top-k 20), so answers vary; pass a seed to repeat one.

test_examples.question: Is this sequence more likely coding or non-coding? Answer in one or two sentences.
test_examples.context: Human HBB (beta-globin), the first 55 bases of the coding sequence on the plus strand.
